MetaCheck Report

ECG foundation models share an age-related performance disparity that originates in the data, not the models

2026-11-22 · Metacheck 0.4.4.29 · DOI 10.64898/2026.10.30.26366943

3to fix3to check0to decide by hand1fine8not applicable

To fix (3)

To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 410 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 1 of 2856 data columns (0%) is documented in a codebook; 2855 are not.
  • A codebook was found and parsed (410 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents panel, backbone, backbone_label while the data has arch, median_seed_sd, max_seed_sd. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 25 codebook/README/label sources and 2856 data columns across 174 files.

A codebook was found and parsed (410 variable definitions), but its variable names do not match the data columns, so the documentation could not be linked automatically (only 0% of columns matched). For example, the codebook documents panel, backbone, backbone_label while the data has arch, median_seed_sd, max_seed_sd. This often means the data holds computed scores or subscales while the codebook lists the underlying items. To make the codebook usable automatically, document variables under the exact names used in the data file (one row per data column), with a label and, for rating items, the response scale.

README files were found in all repositories.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 554 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (554). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory, .Rapp.history) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp, an interrupted save of R’s workspace, .RDataTmp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

To check (3)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 2 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p=0.54 Older patients are not scarce (Emory: 205,701 ECGs at ≥75), and increasing the labelled set from 3,000 ECGs to the full set raised AUROC by 0.016 (p=0.0001) but changed the gap by only -0.010 (Holm-adjusted p=0.54; Fig. 4B).
p=1.0 Group-robust optimisation [23], class balancing, per-age-band probes and focal reweighting changed the gap by medians of +0.000, +0.000, +0.003 and +0.002 (all adjusted p=1.0) while costing overall AUROC (-0.005 to -0.171; Fig. 4C), and a non-linear per-band read-out never recovered the oldest band (avoidable gain -0.025 to -0.001; Fig. 4D).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 29 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 18 distinct packages/libraries: build_classical_figure, csv, figstyle, figstyle_helpers, geopandas, glob, json, math, matplotlib, numpy, os, pandas, pypdf, re, scipy, shutil, sys, v2_checks. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

Without one, the package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and they may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Share the underlying data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable) with a codebook: ne_110m_admin_0_countries.VERSION.txt. We ran automated data-quality checks on 2856 columns; 76 columns have at least one potential issue (62 columns whose name contains file-illegal characters or is excessively long; 4 columns with inconsistent category casing; 4 columns that look like geographic coordinates; 4 columns with numeric values stored as text; 2 columns with no observed values (entirely empty)). We detected demographic columns for Age, Gender, Race.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 174 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

A function or option has changed since you wrote the code, so it stops with today’s version of the package.

  1. In R, run renv::init() in your project and add the renv.lock file this creates to the deposit; in Python, run pip freeze > requirements.txt and add that file.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 50 scripts: 33 ran without error, 15 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 2 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: release_bundle_v1/figS06_island/build/figstyle.py (by island_figure.py); build_classical_figure.py (by release_bundle_v1/figS14_classicalgap/build.py, release_bundle_v1/figS13_classicalbands/build.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt). 6 scripts looked for 7 files in another folder than the deposit has them, so before running them once more we copied them there: release_bundle_v1/fig1_cohorts/data/cohort_n_final.json to release_bundle_v1/fig1_cohorts/cohort_n_final.json for Fig1_study_scope_final.py; release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/r1final/classical/classical_age_band_results.csv to release_bundle_v1/inputs/classical_age_band_results.csv for release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/build.py; release_bundle_v1/fig4_mitigation/figure/Fig4.pdf to release_bundle_v1/fig4_mitigation/out/Fig4.pdf for release_bundle_v1/fig4_mitigation/build.py; release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/figure/Fig5.pdf to release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/out/Fig5.pdf for release_bundle_v1/fig5_controls/build.py; release_bundle_v1/figS11_null/figure/FigS_null_bands.pdf to release_bundle_v1/figS11_null/out/FigS_null_bands.pdf for release_bundle_v1/figS11_null/build.py; release_bundle_v1/figS04_adjgap/figure/FigS_adjacent_band_gap.pdf to release_bundle_v1/figS04_adjgap/out/FigS_adjacent_band_gap.pdf for release_bundle_v1/figS04_adjgap/build.py; release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/figure/FigS_classical_age_matched.png to release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/out/FigS_classical_age_matched.png for release_bundle_v1/figS15_classicalmatched/build.py. Building paths from the top of the project (as with here::here()), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

os.chdir() in the code

3 scripts call os.chdir(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with pass. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring an os.chdir() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

Ethics Approval Check

An ethics approval statement was detected, based on the following text:

LEAD (Lung, hEart, sociAl, boDy) is a prospective observational population-based registry (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01727518) approved by the Ethics Committee of the City of Vienna (EK-11-117-0711).

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:
